children.text: Freedom of movement speaks to the strength of a passport! Georgia's neighbors - Turkey, Russia, Azerbaijan, and Armenia - each operate under different visa regimes. Citizens of some of these countries can enter most of the world visa-free, while for others, every trip is a significant visa challenge.
In today's blog, we take a detailed look at our neighboring countries and their freedom of movement, examining where their citizens can travel visa-free and how many countries are open to them.

The Azerbaijani passport offers its holders a certain degree of freedom, but is also marked by significant visa restrictions. While Azerbaijani citizens can travel relatively freely to several neighboring and Asian states, obtaining a visa for travel to most of the world's countries remains a challenge for them.

This "dual reality" of the passport stems from Azerbaijan's geopolitical position. On one hand, Azerbaijani citizens move freely within Turkey, Russia, and former Soviet Union countries; on the other hand, entry into most Western countries requires obtaining a visa.

More precisely, Azerbaijani passport holders can travel visa-free to 34 countries, obtain a visa on arrival in 49 countries, use an eTA in 3 countries, while 112 countries require them to obtain a visa in advance

Turkey's visa regime reflects its geopolitical position and international relations. While Turkish citizens have fairly broad travel opportunities, there are still countries where a visa remains necessary.

The Turkish passport offers its holders fairly broad travel opportunities. Turkish citizens can travel visa-free to 69 countries, which is a fairly high figure. In addition, a visa can be obtained on arrival in 51 countries, further simplifying travel. An eTA (Electronic Travel Authorization) can also be obtained for 6 countries. However, there are 72 countries where Turkish citizens need to obtain a visa in advance.

Russia's visa regime is influenced by several factors, including the country's international relations, geopolitical position, and security considerations. Russia's relationship with Western countries and international sanctions limit the travel opportunities of Russian citizens. At the same time, Russia's influence over former Soviet Union countries and certain Asian countries supports the existence of visa-free regimes in that direction.

The Russian passport offers its holders a certain degree of travel freedom, though it is also marked by visa restrictions. Russian citizens can travel visa-free to 77 countries, reflecting the country's geopolitical influence. A visa can be obtained on arrival in 43 countries, while 7 countries require an eTA (Electronic Travel Authorization). However, there are 72 countries where Russian citizens need to obtain a visa in advance.

Armenia's visa regime depends on many factors, including the country's geopolitical environment, regional tensions, and international relations. Tense relations with Azerbaijan and Turkey, as well as Russia's influence in the South Caucasus, significantly limit the travel opportunities of Armenian citizens. Added to this are the country's economic challenges and political situation, which also affect the strength of its passport.

Today, an Armenian passport allows visa-free travel to only 34 countries. 46 countries issue a visa on arrival, while 3 require electronic authorization (eTA). Meanwhile, 115 countries have made obtaining a visa in advance mandatory for Armenian citizens. These figures place the Armenian passport in a relatively weak position globally.
